title: 250 Rights Groups Demand Probe After Canada Border Agents Target Indian Students at Protest
excerpt: Amnesty International and other organizations are calling for an investigation after CBSA officers checked immigration status and issued removal orders to students protesting work permit denials at a Calgary demonstration.
body:
• More than 250 organizations, including Amnesty International and Greenpeace, have demanded an independent investigation into Canada Border Services Agency actions at a Calgary student protest on August 12.
  • CBSA officers checked 20 protesters' immigration status, directed 12 to a border office, and issued 10 removal orders the same day — while Federal Court challenges were still pending.
  • Approximately 1,500 graduates, predominantly Indian students from Punjab, had their post-graduation work permits retroactively denied after the government excluded 'non-credit' programs in June 2026.
  • The rights groups are calling for suspension of removal orders, an investigation, and assessment of applications under the rules in place when students enrolled.

More than 250 civil liberties, human rights, and labour organizations have called on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to launch an independent investigation into border enforcement actions against Indian students during a peaceful protest in Calgary last month.

The coalition, which includes Amnesty International Canada, Greenpeace, and the Canadian Union of Public Employees, sent an open letter to federal and provincial officials on September 2 describing the August 12 enforcement operation as an unprecedented use of immigration enforcement at a student protest.

What Happened on August 12

The demonstration in Calgary's Saddle Ridge neighbourhood was the fourth and final in a series of protests that began on July 24. Around 1,500 international students — predominantly from Punjab, India — had launched demonstrations and a hunger strike after their post-graduation work permit (PGWP) applications were retroactively rejected.

Calgary Police said officers were called to the protest over complaints about sidewalk obstruction and structures erected without a permit. Police informed demonstrators of their right to protest and asked for identification while addressing bylaw violations. They then contacted the Canada Border Services Agency.

According to CBSA's own account, officers checked 20 protesters, directed 12 to a CBSA office, and issued 10 removal orders the same day. Officers also seized passports. The removal orders were issued while some students had Federal Court challenges still pending and were within their 90-day status restoration period.

"I followed every rule. I paid my tuition, completed my studies and graduated. When I enrolled, we understood that the program qualified for a post-graduation work permit. After we graduated, the federal government refused our applications."

— Gurparas Singh, Portage College graduate

The Policy Change at the Core

The dispute centres on graduates of non-credit vocational programs delivered through public-private partnerships at Portage College campuses across Alberta. Students enrolled in 2024 under the understanding that their programs qualified for PGWPs. Graduates of the same programs in earlier years had received permits.

On June 24, 2026, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) added language to its website excluding 'non-credit' programs from PGWP eligibility. That term appeared in no regulation, Canada Gazette notice, or Ministerial Instruction before that date. As many as 1,500 graduates were affected, with hundreds already refused after paying more than $30,000 in tuition.

Newly uncovered emails, first reported by PressProgress, show that students asked about their eligibility while still enrolled. Federal guidance provided to the college said currently enrolled students would not be affected and told them to continue their programs.

Coalition Demands

The 250-plus organizations are making four demands: an independent investigation into the actions of Calgary Police and CBSA on August 12; immediate suspension of the removal orders; clear public policies preventing immigration enforcement from being triggered by protest participation; and assessment of Portage College graduates' applications under the rules in place when they enrolled.

"People should not have to choose between speaking out against injustice and protecting their ability to remain in Canada. Targeting peaceful protests strikes fear into the heart of entire communities."

— Julia Sande, Amnesty International Canada

Political Response

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith defended the enforcement approach, stating that international students are in Canada temporarily and that immigration rules must be followed. Prime Minister Carney has also previously said people without authorization to remain should follow the applicable legal process.

Immigration lawyer Jatin Shory, who represents roughly a dozen students challenging their work permit denials in Federal Court, said he had advised clients against attending protests. Immigration lawyer Joycna Kang of the Canadian Immigration Lawyers' Association called the CBSA action 'surprising,' noting the agency's enforcement powers are generally tied to border points rather than interior locations.

IRCC has not announced any reconsideration or policy reversal as of this writing. A petition calling on Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab to pause all PGWP refusals on Portage College files remains active.
nri_angle: Indian students, predominantly from Punjab, make up the majority of the 1,500 Portage College graduates affected by retroactive work permit rule changes in Canada.
